text.p: ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG said it had successfully installed the world's first commercially operational high-temperature superconducting device for an electrical utility service.
ABB said the device, installed in a Swiss hyroelectrcial plant, was a current limiter designed to protect equipment and personnel against the effects of short-circuit electrical faults.
The device uses the superconductor's unique properties of extreme cooling to dampen the current surge caused by a short-circuit.
"The installaction of such devices reduces the damage caused by electrical faults, shortens repair time and provides utility personnel with greater security," an ABB statement said.
"The result for electrical compnaies is greater power supply reliability and lower operating costs," it added.
ABB said the current limiter now installed was the world's first in commercial operation at a power plant.
ABB said the so-called "fault current limit" would undergo long-term performance monitoring under actual operating conditions starting today.
"With a rating of 1 megavolt-ampere (MVA) at a system voltage of 10.5 kilovolts, it is also the most pwerful device of its kind in the world," ABB said.
ABB said it was a "high-temperature" device, meaning it is cooled to 77 degrees Kelvin rather than earlier "low-temperature" devices which had to be cooled to around four degrees Kelvin.
Kelvin is a temperature scale whose zero point is the same as what scientists call "absolute zero", or minus 273 degrees Celsius.
The installation was at a hydro plant named Kraftwerk am Loentsch near Glarus in central Switzerland, owned by Swiss utility Nordostschweizerische Kraftwerke AG (NOK).
Financial support for the commercial development and testing of the device was provided by a Swiss utility studies fund and practical assistance was leant by NOK, ABB said.
